before.exam_tip_html: When you encounter an unfamiliar 19th-century word, do not waste time worrying about it. Read the sentence around it, work out the general meaning from context, and move on. The examiner rewards analysis of how language creates effects, not vocabulary quizzes. You can write an excellent analytical paragraph about a word’s effect even if you are not 100% certain of its dictionary definition.

When a question asks you to discuss themes, do not just list them. The examiner wants to see you explain how the writer develops the theme. Always follow this pattern: identify the theme, provide a quotation, analyse the writer’s method, and explain the effect on the reader. Top-band answers link multiple methods to the same theme, showing how different techniques work together.

For the 10-mark language analysis question, aim for three or four detailed analytical points rather than six or seven shallow ones. Each point should follow the pattern: quotation, technique, connotation, effect. Use subject terminology naturally — do not force-fit technique names. The examiners reward quality of analysis over quantity of observations. Always explore connotations — what words suggest beyond their literal meaning.

Before writing your review, jot down 3 specific details you will describe and whether each will be praised or criticised. This gives you a ready-made structure and ensures your review has both positive and negative elements. Use sensory detail in at least one paragraph — the examiner rewards description that makes the experience feel real.

Do not waste time in the exam trying to identify the exact genre of the extract. Instead, let the text guide your analysis. If the writing is dark and atmospheric, focus on how the writer creates fear and unease. If it is grounded and realistic, focus on subtle characterisation and social context. The examiners are looking for analytical skill, not genre classification.
